commits.summary: tool_time.py: where loops' time went, by category, loop and cargo test binary, from the redacted logs
commits.body:
Phase 1 step 1 of the test-cost brief (llm-dlc/loops/test-cost.md). llm-dlc/tools/tool_time.py turns the 2026-11-15 ad-hoc time analysis, whose scripts were not kept, into a tool Phase 5 runs again on the next loop. It finds loop sessions from the briefs' Loop settings and the loop summaries (a stream counts towards its loop), reads each session's redacted log (with --fetch, the published copy of one not stored here, checked against its sha256), and reports: active and model time (metrics.py's), blocked time per batch of parallel calls (counted once, given to the call that finished last, calls over two hours left out) by category, waits on commands started in the background, per-loop shares, cargo's compile and per-binary test timings, and full-suite, debug and release spreads. Markdown or --format json.

Verified: test_tool_time.py (10 tests on made-up logs: classification, batching, the two-hour cut, background waits by task id and by redirected file, cargo output parsing, full-suite detection, discovery, an end-to-end JSON report, and fetch refusing content that doesn't match its name) and test_metrics.py pass. Run on the measurement's 26 sessions it reproduces the compile/test split exactly (936 timed runs, 0.9h compiling, 8.2h tests) and the slow files' order (conformance.rs, observations.rs, integration.rs, alignment.rs, application_core.rs).

The brief is out of date in places: its 'Where it starts from' totals came from those scripts, under other definitions. This tool gives active 116h, tools 47.8h, cargo test 20.8h, proofs inline 4.7h; and for full-suite debug runs 91 calls, 14% of cargo test time, median 11s, p90 579s, against the brief's 542 runs, 48%, median 17s and p90 136s (all debug runs: 788, 44%, median 8s, p90 82s). It finds 26 loop sessions, not 27. Done-when's 60-second budget is unaffected; Phase 5 should compare against this tool's numbers. Progress records the command line.

commits.summary: test_costs.py: the per-test cost measuring tool, written and tested but not run; cargo-nextest installed, hash-pinned
commits.body: Phase 1 step 2 of the test-cost brief, as revised after the user stopped the run before its measuring job. lib/tools/test_costs.py measures what each test costs: a warm plain cargo test for the default run's wall time, then every Rust test under cargo-nextest, one process each (debug for default tests, release for ignored ones), and every Python test file test by test. For each test it records time, CPU, peak memory and the processes spawned (sampled from /proc), and writes lib/tests/costs.json with the tier each test measures into (unit: no subprocess, under 1 s; tool: under 10 s and 1 GB; proof: JBMC/TLC or over those). lib/.config/nextest.toml defines only a measure profile that runs each test under the tool's watch wrapper; plain cargo test and nextest's default profile are unaffected. lib/tools/install-nextest.sh installs cargo-nextest 0.9.151 from its github.com release, pinned to the sha256 that both the release's .sha256 asset and GitHub's asset digest give.

commits.summary: test_costs.py estimate: the cost inventory of every Rust and Python test, from past runs and what each test calls, running nothing
commits.body:
lib/tests/costs.json is now generated by `python3 lib/tools/test_costs.py estimate` (about 20 s, no test run). It lists the 642 Rust tests and 782 Python tests, one per line, each with a tier, what it calls, its cost and that cost's sources, and why. A new module, lib/tools/cost_inventory.py, does the reading:
- The Rust tests come from lib/src and lib/tests with strings and comments blanked. The list matched `cargo test -- --list` exactly, a check run once that only lists. The Python tests come from ast.
- What a test calls is read from its body and the same-file helpers it reaches: JBMC through Engine::Jbmc or Auto, equivalence::run or property::run without the native engine, has_jbmc() or missing("JBMC"); TLC through run_tlc or tlc_command; javac, java, the binary, a stand-in script, or Command::new.
- What a test cost comes from the cargo output kept in 22 redacted session logs, through tool_time.py, and from 52 past jobs' logs in verification/results. A section that ran one test gives that test's time, one that ran several bounds each of them, and "running for over 60 seconds" bounds a test from below. Python's comes from runs of a single file or test.

A test's tier is the higher of what it calls and what it took alone. A tier no past run settles is marked estimated, with the reason. A proof-tier test that runs by default is marked retier: pending.
- Rust: 268 unit, 299 tool and 75 proof. The proof tests are the 12 ignored ones and 63 retier pending, 45 of those in integration.rs. 226 Rust tiers are estimates.
- Python: 611 unit, 171 tool, no proof, and 394 estimates.

The brief asked for lib/tests/costs.json "and the same for Python": both are in that one file, as the rust and python lists.

Known gap, left to the next loop: measure's inventory still keys rows by nextest's binary id, so it must be made to write the same shape before it replaces these estimates.

commits.summary: Test tiers: the lint, test_costs.py lint, in the default run as tests/tiers.rs and tools/test_tier_lint.py
commits.body:
Phase 2 step 7 of llm-dlc/loops/test-cost.md. The lint checks four things against the sources and lib/tests/costs.json: every ignore reason is a cost:proof tag with a proxy that runs by default, or proxy: none yet for a test on the inventory's list; no test outside the proof tier calls JBMC or TLC, except the retier: pending tests; the inventory and the sources name the same tests, and what it records of each is current; and every tool_tier! or @cost tag is the one its row asks for. Joining the retier: pending or proxy: none yet list is now for a person: estimate keeps the tests already listed. A new JBMC or TLC test that runs by default, or a new proxy: none yet, gets an unlisted row, which the lint refuses until a person runs estimate --list FILE::NAME. A Python proof tag now carries its reason, @cost("proof", "...; proxy: Class.test"), and the lint refuses an unconditional @unittest.skip. The Python listing now follows a TestCase base imported from another file of the repository. commits.summary: sync: metrics of sessions traced in another workspace follow the price list; Fable 5.2 priced, Sonnet 5.5 cache reads corrected
commits.body:
sync could recompute metrics.json only for sessions whose transcript is in this checkout's Claude project folder. The merged streams' sessions keep theirs in their own workspaces' folders, named after those paths, so a price change left their metrics.json stale and check failed on them (17 sessions, seen and reverted in the previous two commits). sync now ends its session loop with refresh_metrics: every session with a manifest but no transcript here gets its metrics.json recomputed from its stored log and manifest, exactly as check recomputes it. This happens once for each set of logs, recorded in the sync cache, whose fingerprint already covers pricing.json and the tools, so a price or metrics.py change recomputes them all. A session whose log isn't stored here is left as it is. Only metrics.json is written: summaries carry no costs.

With that, llm-dlc/pricing.json gets the change it waited for: claude-fable-5-2 at $8 input and $40 output per million tokens, $0.20 cache reads, and $10 and $16 cache writes (the file's 1.25x and 2x), and claude-sonnet-5-5's cache read at its list $0.10 instead of $0.20. as_of is 2026-11-15. Session 0c1ceb11's Fable 5.2 calls no longer count as $0.

Verified: a new unit test, Checks.test_metrics_of_a_session_traced_in_another_workspace_follow_the_prices, covers recomputing, not re-reading the same logs, recomputing under new prices, skipping a session whose transcript is here, and leaving one whose log is missing. commits.summary: feature-loop.sh: moonshots, and templated moonshots that take one item of a list per cycle, starting with prove-examples (285-300)
commits.body:
The one-line named instructions of the repo's first days (features, tla, spring, relational) are now called moonshots, apart from briefs and their streams. A templated moonshot puts the next item of its list into its template each cycle: prove-examples gives examples 285 to 300 in turn to "Formally prove example {} as elegantly and efficiently as possible", in a session of its own fixed in the script (a4ac2b6c-a5b9-4507-a21e-1b56ae8b2c31) on claude-fable-5-2 at high effort, which the first run creates and later runs resume. An item is done once an earlier run's record in llm-dlc/loop-summaries lists a commit for it ('- cycle N, item X, ...'), so a run starts at the first item without one, runs at most as many cycles as items are left, and ends when the list does. pricing.json gains claude-fable-5-2 at its list price (8/40 per MTok, cache read 0.20).

Verified with a stub claude in a throwaway jj repo: the first turn created the session with --session-id on claude-fable-5-2 at high effort and every later turn resumed it; a 3-cycle run took 285-287; a run whose cycle made no commit stopped and left 288; the next run took 288-289; with every item recorded the loop exits 0 without calling claude.

commits.summary: Loop statistics: every loop added up by category, loop, run, cycle and item, with the history back to 2026-11-01
commits.body:
llm-dlc/traces/loops.json and loops.md are new generated files: what the unattended loops cost and produced. A new module, llm-dlc/tools/loop_stats.py, adds up moonshots, briefs with their streams, and the verification loop, each by loop, run and cycle: time (elapsed and active), tokens, cost at list price, commits, compactions and context, and the verification jobs each cycle submitted with their final result and compute. A templated moonshot such as prove-examples also gets a row per item: its attempts, what they cost, its commit, and whether its proof passed. sync.py writes both files on every sync, check fails when either is stale, regenerate settles them after a merge, and the publication gate covers them. If the statistics cannot be computed, the files say why, the commit goes on and check warns.

The data was already there, in each session's metrics.json (every prompt with its time, tokens and cost); nothing said which prompts were a loop's. A run with a published record owns the prompts of its session between its Started and end lines; the n-th instruction is cycle n and, in a templated moonshot, takes the n-th item of the header's list. The 8 runs with no published record (all before 2026-11-06: the moonshots features, tla, spring and relational, and the briefs sync-performance, build-orchestration and sound-verdicts) are read from their sessions' prompts and marked source: transcript. They are split where a person typed, after 30 minutes without a turn, at the closing summary, and where the script's count of cycles starts over. History as extracted: 4 moonshots (46 cycles, 43 with a commit, $522), 26 brief loops in 51 runs (289 cycles, $1,078), and 49 verification-loop sessions ($15); 235 of 280 verification jobs are tied to the cycle that submitted them.

Three changes make the data sufficient from here on. feature-loop.sh writes a record's times in UTC whatever the machine's zone, since they are matched against the transcript's, and names the item in the line for a cycle that made no commit. pipeline.py submit records the session Claude Code runs it in when --session is not given, so a job is tied to its cycle without relying on the commit message. Records with a zone the reader cannot place are read as UTC and listed on the page.

Verified: test_loop_stats.py (18 tests, new) on made-up sessions, records and jobs; the other llm-dlc tool suites (test_performance 103, test_runs, test_workspaces, test_metrics, test_review, test_streams_status, test_prune_workspaces) and verification/test_pipeline.py (35, one new). On the real history, every one of the 47 published records agrees with what was read from its session: the same number of cycles as its end line says, and a commit line for exactly the cycles found committed. feature-loop.sh was run against a stub claude in a throwaway jj repo with TZ=America/New_York: its records carried UTC times and parsed, including the no-commit stop. This commit was made in the moonshot workspace, on main plus uklpttst: when it moves onto the default line, run sync.py regenerate (the two files are computed from the sessions and records on that line), and tag the new tests with lib/tools/test_costs.py, which does not exist here.

commits.summary: Loop statistics: the loop a person ran by hand on 2026-10-31 counted as a moonshot of its own kind, and a cycle's commits held to its own turns
commits.body:
examples-by-hand is a new loop in llm-dlc/traces/loops.json and loops.md: the three cycles a person typed on the evening of 2026-10-31, before feature-loop.sh existed. Each was an instruction (reworded each time, for another audience), a commit (the Quorum, Crosscut and Mica example families) and a typed /compact, which is the cycle the script was written that night to automate. It is read from the session's prompts like the other runs with no record: 3 cycles, 3 commits, 2 h 34 min active, $55.22 at list price. It counts with the moonshots, and is kept apart by a kind of its own, moonshot by hand, on every row; the page marks it in the moonshots table, lists its three wordings, says under the totals that the moonshot row includes it, and explains what differs: no script capped a cycle, checked for a commit or compacted for it, and a person chose each instruction after reading the last result. The user asked for it to be counted, with a disclaimer.

A cycle's commits are now those its session made during the cycle's turns. Before, the last cycle of a run also took commits stamped on the session afterwards, while it sat idle: another session's work, or a person's allow-list approval. That had given six cycles 9 commits too many (574 in all, now 569 before the three by hand), and had counted the last build-orchestration cycle as committed when the loop had stopped on it without a commit. All 47 published records still agree with what is read from their sessions.

Verified: test_loop_stats.py (20 tests, two new: the hand-run loop, and a commit stamped on an idle session), the other llm-dlc tool suites, and sync.py check at 0 errors and 0 warnings. Made in the moonshot workspace, on tkvkkllx: after the move onto the default line, run sync.py regenerate.
